📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

Industry observers note that an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that highlights up in the fresh RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

It has been revealed that every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, owners of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a newly introduced paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

According to recent reports, we think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it.".

Industry observers note that the frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

Sources indicate that the RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

According to recent reports, framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:.

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

According to recent reports, A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

In a recent development, harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

According to recent reports, here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

Recent findings suggest that the command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:.

Industry observers note that A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

It has been revealed that the best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:.

Industry observers note that that is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

The docs have the full reference.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment highlights up in the filter.

Recent findings suggest that the first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:.

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your owners publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

Breaking: Local AI Agents in Power Electronics Simulation: Deployment, Measurements and Costs

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (263 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.24880v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging in power electronics, where it drives the simulation loop that engineers used to close largely by hand. In this loop, a converter design, or a study of the network it connects to, is built, run, measured and revised until it satisfies its specification. Such an agent can be served from a cloud API or from an inference device on the premises. For organizations whose designs, customer data or export-controlled material cannot leave the site, and whose simulators are licensed there, local deployment is the natural choice. In such a deployment, the agent becomes an electrical load on the organization's own equipment, i.e., every run consumes power and energy on a local device, generates tokens and takes time. However, existing work focuses mainly on what the agent can achieve with cloud-hosted models. What a local deployment costs in power, energy, tokens and time on real simulation tasks, and what its choices trade against one another, has received little quantitative investigation under comparable conditions. To address this gap, a systematic evaluation framework is presented in this paper. It applies locally served models to agentic power electronics tasks, from the converter level to the system level, and measures their power, energy, token and time costs. Based on these measurements, the capability boundary of a local agent on such tasks and the cost per solved task are characterized. The results are expected to provide practical insight for the use of agentic AI in power electronics and the power systems it serves.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (255 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.24869v2 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arva AI, a tech giant that deploys AI agents to make critical banking decisions, has secured $20m in Series A funding as it looks to push its accuracy-focused technology deeper into the bank back office.

Arthur Ventures led the round, and existing backers Y Combinator and Gradient also took part.

According to recent reports, according to the tech giant, most back-office decisions at banks are still made manually, but this has begun to shift. Over the past year, Arva’s customers started entrusting vital decisions to its agents, with staff setting policies and monitoring outcomes.

During that period the firm rolled out its technology at scale with banks and FinTechs, among them a top-10 US bank, a payments institution listed on the S&P 500 and the global FinTech Wise.

It has been revealed that arva argues that accuracy is the deciding factor in how much work a bank can delegate to AI. Areas such as financial crime compliance, onboarding, payment operations and lending generate a constant stream of decisions, most of which are still reviewed individually as backlogs grow. For AI to take on this work, banks must be able to trust each result and justify it to regulators. The tech giant indicates general-purpose models fall short on both counts, lacking the required precision and often being unable to explain their reasoning.

Recent findings suggest that arva’s agents manage critical decisions from beginning to end across compliance, onboarding, payments and lending. The firm believes high accuracy depends on its models, agents and learning systems operating in tandem.

Sources indicate that in September it set up Arva Research, an in-house lab developing proprietary models for the most accuracy-sensitive stages of a decision. Its agents draw on these models to process each case, while AgentCore, the firm’s continual learning infrastructure, tailors them to a given bank’s operations and policies over time.

Arva Intel, the lab’s debut model, carries out in-depth online research into individuals and businesses, and beat leading general-purpose models on accuracy by 13% in the organization’s testing.

The latest capital will support Arva Research’s development of further models and the expansion of AgentCore. Arva also intends to extend its agents to additional decision types, such as disputes, payment operations and lending.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connect Money, an Egypt-based FinTech offering embedded finance and white-label card services, has secured $3.5m in a pre-Series A round as it gears up to take its platform into Saudi Arabia and Morocco.

The round was led by returning backers Mohamed Farouk, Algebra Ventures and DisrupTech Ventures, according to a report from Wamda. The deal blends new funding with the sale of secondary shares, giving a number of the startup’s early backers a partial exit. Connect Money has not revealed what portion of the $3.5m is new capital.

It has been revealed that the organization will use the money to move into its two new target markets, with obtaining regulatory sign-off and building the necessary infrastructure being the main priorities. In Saudi Arabia, the firm is pursuing a licence from the Saudi Central Bank (SAMA). In Morocco, it is putting in place local operations and technology systems, with a commercial launch pencilled in for the first half of 2027.

It has been revealed that the move will take Connect Money’s embedded finance offering outside its home market for the first time. It is aimed at businesses that want to provide payment products to their customers but would rather not build banking infrastructure themselves.

Sources indicate that connect Money states it has issued more than 300,000 cards so far. The platform aims to help businesses reach customers who rely on cash by giving them access to digital payments, instant lending tools and a network of more than 20,000 marketplace partners.

The firm takes care of the complicated parts of card issuance, so that companies can launch their own banking proposition through white-label cards paired with a digital banking app. Connect Money says this lets clients skip long regulatory processes, large upfront spending and continuing operational costs. It also says businesses can open up new banking-related revenue streams without any initial investment.

Amazon WorkSpaces Applications adds support for smart card redirection

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, amazon WorkSpaces Applications now supports smart card redirection on single-session and multi-session fleets, so consumers can access the smart card connected to their local device from applications inside their streaming session.
  • Sources indicate that administrators can turn smart card sign-in for Active Directory and smart card redirection on or off independently for each stack.
  • These capabilities are available today in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) regions that offer WorkSpaces Applications.

According to recent reports, amazon WorkSpaces Applications now supports smart card redirection on single-session and multi-session fleets, so consumers can access the smart card connected to their local device from applications inside their streaming session. It also extends smart card sign-in, previously limited to single-session fleets, to multi-session fleets. This launch helps public sector, healthcare, and other regulated organizations that use Common Access Card (CAC) or Personal Identity Verification (PIV) cards run those workflows on multi-session fleets.

Sources indicate that administrators can turn smart card sign-in for Active Directory and smart card redirection on or off independently for each stack. Smart card sign-in lets users sign in to domain-joined streaming instances with their smart card instead of a password, while redirected smart cards support in-session authentication, digital signing, and email encryption. For example, a government agency can move CAC users from single-session to multi-session fleets and keep CAC sign-in.

These capabilities are available today in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) regions that offer WorkSpaces Applications.

According to recent reports, to get started, turn on either setting under User settings for your stack, use a Windows image with the latest WorkSpaces Applications agent, and connect with the WorkSpaces Applications client for Windows. Upcoming stacks have both settings turned off by default, and existing stacks that use smart card redirection keep it turned on. To learn more, see Create a stack in the Amazon WorkSpaces Applications Administration Guide, or visit the Amazon WorkSpaces Applications product page.

Tech Report: Holo4: powering generalist computer-use agents

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1372 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Holo4 is our upcoming series of agentic models.
  • In a recent development, holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs.
  • In a recent development, holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Holo4 is our upcoming series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

In a recent development, holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

In a recent development, holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Industry observers note that holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Sources indicate that holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

AutomationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

Sources indicate that the tower is square in proposal at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

Four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Holo4 27B (84 calls, 1.3M tokens).

Qwen3.8 27B (60 calls, 1.0M tokens).

Recent findings suggest that build a 3D model in FreeCAD of the H tech giant logo: a solid filled disc beside a blocky sans-serif capital letter H, both extruded to the same thickness, the two shapes of similar height and set apart so they do not overlap, with the centre of the disc level with the middle of the H. Colour both shapes black.

Holo4 27B (94 calls, 1.5M tokens).

Qwen3.8 27B (118 calls, 1.9M tokens).

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

According to recent reports, A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

Industry observers note that no one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines).

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines).

Our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Sources indicate that alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Industry observers note that opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Industry observers note that our post-training stack is designed to adapt to fresh foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

Industry observers note that these gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Sources indicate that both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Managing Director, Global Partner Marketing.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

At Google Cloud, our commitment to agentic transformation extends to everyone, including the partners who build and grow alongside us.

Today, we are excited to introduce latest Gemini-powered co-marketing capabilities directly within everyday go-to-market workflows for our partners. These new features enable partners to produce customized, brand-aligned joint assets in minutes, scaling campaign execution and driving pipeline more effectively.

In a recent development, as technology evolves and customer expectations shift, marketers are no longer just producing campaigns. We’re building continuous, hyper-personalized, data-driven demand engines, and we’re doing it across an increasingly fragmented buyer journey.

For our partner network, delivering on this expectation means solving a dual challenge: differentiating core offerings while articulating a unified vision with Google Cloud.

Bridging that gap at enterprise scale requires more than incremental efficiency — it requires agentic agility to jointly create, adapt, and distribute stories together that resonate.

The updated Partner Marketing Studio introduces a suite of agentic tools designed to accelerate campaign execution, optimize performance, and maximize impact for partners of all sizes.

Agentic search: Partners can now use a simple chat feature. Search for what you need, rather than navigating a content repository.

Brand alignment: Never worry about brand compliance again, with a brand reviewer agent that helps ensure your content upholds Google Cloud’s partner brand guidelines.

ISV asset creation: Gemini generated, high-fidelity marketing assets to drive demand to marketplace listings.

Social automation: A newly introduced social editor with the ability to create posts across multiple networks simultaneously, add account tags, and refine messaging per channel with AI.

Customer case studies: An agent designed to build best-in-class customer success stories to highlight joint customer wins.

Gemini-Assisted Translation: Accelerate global marketing programs with agentic translations across 130 languages.

Natural language analytics: Gain end-to-end visibility connecting marketing execution directly to tangible business outcomes.

In a recent development, "Partner Marketing Studio has become an extension of our partner marketing team. With built-in Gemini capabilities and ready-to-run joint campaigns, we can tailor high-impact marketing assets across industries, regions, and personas in minutes. It allows us to do more with less while accelerating pipeline for our joint solutions" - Liana Shuma, Global Head of Technology Partnerships, Pigment.

While the platform features powerful latest tools, our core focus remains unchanged: helping you build your brand authority and generate pipeline demand.

It has been revealed that you will continue to find a curated content library structured specifically for you, highlighting top-performing campaigns aligned with Google Cloud strategic priority plays. Partners maintain full access to Google-produced localized campaign content and ready-made assets that can be customized to suit specific go-to-market objectives.

Furthermore, high-value partner services remain readily accessible within the platform:.

Applying to host customer events directly inside a Google office.

Requesting a Google Cloud speaker for your hosted events.

Attending dedicated office-hours sessions with Google Cloud marketing experts.

Requesting social amplification for campaigns.

According to recent reports, “Google offices are not only a great draw for attendees, but by handling all event logistics, Google Cloud saved us significant time, money, and allowed us to focus entirely on delivering high-impact content and driving audience engagement” - Jenny Bejarano. GTM Specialist, Tiger Analytics.

According to recent reports, “We appreciate Google Cloud’s support with speakers for our events. This collaboration strengthens our credibility and value proposition with prospects” - Tommaso Vaccarella, Co-Founder & General Manager, Connected Stories.

Via Google Cloud Partner Network: Navigate to Resources > Marketing > Partner Marketing Studio.

Via direct browser link: Visit www.partnermarketingstudio.com directly.

These updates are part of Google Cloud’s larger commitment to transforming how we empower and enable partners with Gemini. In addition to Partner Marketing Studio, we’re leveraging Gemini throughout the partner experience, including a revamped partner marketing funds experience to streamline activity planning, simplify pipeline reporting, and proactively validate required documentation before submission.

In a recent development, we’ve seen Google Cloud experience tremendous growth in recent years, and a major part of that success has been the incredible work done by our partner ecosystem. Now, as we’re bringing the power of Gemini directly into your go-to-market workflows, we’re excited to take our work together to a whole new level.

With AI at our side, and as one of our strongest offerings, it will be easier than ever to create, connect, and grow together.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arcesium, a global technology provider serving the investment sector, has rolled out Arcesium Blue, an integrated, AI-ready platform that gives expanding hedge funds a complete front-to-back setup from the moment they go live.

In a recent development, blue pairs cloud-native software with premium managed services. It is aimed at funds running long/short equity, macro, simple credit or single-strategy books. Its purpose is to spare managers from building complicated operational infrastructure themselves, so they can concentrate on generating returns while they grow.

The platform covers real-time portfolio management, order and execution management, compliance and risk, and post-trade operations, linking each stage of the investment lifecycle in one connected system. Newly debuted and rapidly expanding funds often run into disjointed technology and configuration problems. Blue tackles this with a unified stack backed by experienced, institutional-grade professionals who provide managed services.

According to recent reports, on the front-office side, portfolio managers can monitor P&L in real time, simulate trades and run stress tests. The order management system lets users allocate across asset classes from a single order entry screen. Day-to-day tasks such as reporting, accounting, reconciliations and data management take place within the platform and are overseen by Arcesium’s operations specialists. Compliance and risk processes rely on tight data controls and a full audit trail, so firms work with verified data at every stage.

Industry observers note that the Aquata data platform sits at the core of Blue. It offers ready-made connections to external parties and systems, sophisticated data management tools and support for AI-native workflows, which keeps the front office and operational systems aligned on a single set of figures. Owners also get full access to Arcesium Intelligence, an embedded AI environment that works with any model and includes hundreds of preconfigured agents and applications designed to speed up decision-making.

Because Blue uses a focused scope and standardised configurations, it can be deployed swiftly through one provider. As funds mature and take on more sophisticated strategies, they can move into the broader Arcesium ecosystem for a tailored setup without rebuilding their systems.

Arcesium CEO Gaurav Suri mentioned, “Hedge funds require confidence and trust in the technologies and services that fuel their daily operations. This peace of mind allows managers to focus on what they do best without the constraints of fragmented infrastructure. Blue enables funds to focus on growth, with a full front-to-back offering, AI-readiness, and seasoned experts who take investment operations off their plates.

Introducing object enrichments: Transform unstructured data into agent-ready context

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The vast majority of enterprise information is unstructured, locked away in object storage as petabytes of images, PDFs, videos, and audio files.
  • Today, we are introducing object enrichments, a upcoming Google Cloud Storage capability that uses AI models to automatically extract rich contextual metadata from Cloud Storage objects and saves it in-place as object context, enabling agents to acquire the information needed to make complex business decisions.
  • “L'Oreal is the 4th largest advertiser in the world, and managing media assets at that scale is complex.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

The vast majority of enterprise information is unstructured, locked away in object storage as petabytes of images, PDFs, videos, and audio files. This data holds the institutional knowledge AI agents need to do business-critical work. But to an agent, a raw object is just bytes it can't reason over. As enterprises start to deploy agents in production, the focus has shifted toward transforming these raw objects into rich, agent-ready context.

Today, we are introducing object enrichments, a upcoming Google Cloud Storage capability that uses AI models to automatically extract rich contextual metadata from Cloud Storage objects and saves it in-place as object context, enabling agents to acquire the information needed to make complex business decisions. Object enrichments gives customers access to the AI models used by internal Google services such as Google Photos, offering image annotations like object detection and image labeling at 75% cost savings when compared to similar services from other cloud providers. Available in preview, this fully managed service also includes high-quality PDF classification model, enabling customers to seamlessly turn their object store into an intelligent, AI-ready foundation.

“L'Oreal is the 4th largest advertiser in the world, and managing media assets at that scale is complex. Cloud Storage object enrichments’s high quality and cost-effective annotations enable us to discover, understand, and govern our content at scale, accelerating marketing and advertising operations while remaining compliant in all markets. Object enrichments enables L'Oreal to label its extensive creative asset repository 100x faster at a fraction of the cost of existing pipelines and processes.” – Antoine Castex, Principal Data & AI Architect, L’Oreal.

In a recent development, to operate efficiently, agents need grounded knowledge; however, reading every raw file at scale is cost- and performance-prohibitive. For example, if an operations agent needs to pinpoint a specific event—such as a doorstep package delivery or a roadway hazard—streaming thousands of smart-camera or vehicle frames into the AI model on every user prompt would burn through expensive tokens and add minutes of delay. To bridge this gap, teams must pre-process raw data and extract rich, contextual metadata, which agents can then leverage at runtime. Historically, achieving this meant dealing with three challenges:.

Cost: Running models over millions to billions of objects is expensive, pushing organizations to compromise and process only a fraction of their data, creating blind spots that lessen agents’ accuracy.

In a recent development, operational toil: A self-managed pipeline means stitching together multiple services — from event triggers and queues to custom infrastructure built on Cloud Run or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) — along with scalable retry/error logic and job scheduling. Once deployed, that infrastructure still requires continuous upgrades and capacity management. Teams sometimes spend months on this plumbing rather than focusing on building agents that solve actual business problems.

Recent findings suggest that fragmented metadata: Extracted metadata often lands in a separate data store, decoupling context from the bytes it describes. Teams must pay for and maintain a second storage system, govern access policies across disconnected permission models, and run custom cleanup jobs to keep metadata in sync when source objects are copied, moved, or deleted.

This is why we built object enrichments: to natively provide agent-ready context for your unstructured data, equipping your agents with complete, grounded knowledge without prohibitive costs, custom pipeline plumbing, or fragmented metadata.

Recent findings suggest that 1. Reduce costs with Google modelsObject enrichments offers dramatic savings at scale: enriching 10 million images or PDFs costs just $700 (according to published pricing). You can use Google’s high-quality AI models for image annotations—including object detection, face detection, image labeling, and explicit content detection—at one of the industry’s best price points. In addition, the PDF classification model lets you categorize documents into standard business and industry categories like Finance, Games, News, and Health.

"Even with a highly accurate baseline, Hyperscience leveraged object enrichments to drive a 50%+ lift in document classification accuracy, while simultaneously reducing classification inference costs by 2-3x.” – Mayur Pillay, VP Partnerships, Hyperscience.

2. Generate richer context with GeminiFor complex multimodal reasoning across text, PDFs, images, audio, and video, you can leverage Gemini natively with object enrichments, unlocking advanced use cases such as summarization, entity extraction, transcription, and translation. Please reach out to us at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality.

It has been revealed that 3. No pipeline, low toil setupSkip the brittle, multi-component DIY pipelines. Setting up an enrichment job just takes three simple steps, with no code required in the Google Cloud console, or programmatically via the Cloud Storage API, following these steps:.

It has been revealed that define your scope: Provide a set of buckets containing the objects to process and specify the processing location. Object enrichments can scale to millions or billions of objects.

Choose your models: Pick one or more of the five first-party Cloud Storage models for images and PDFs.

Grant permissions: Grant the necessary IAM permissions to the object enrichments service to access your Cloud Storage buckets.

Object enrichments handles the rest: It orchestrates model inference, parses the responses, and writes the results to each object's object context, with built-in retries and throttling. There are no queues to manage, workers to scale, or glue code to maintain.

"Cloud Storage object enrichments and BigQuery, slashes AI development from 6 months to 1 month while rapidly improving our models." - Brandon Bunker, VP of Product AI, Vivint.

4. Context lives where the bytes liveInstead of parking metadata in a separate data store, object enrichments writes model outputs directly to object context, a specialized Cloud Storage metadata construct that’s purpose-built for storing contextual information as structured key-value pairs alongside the object itself. Because context is stored alongside object’s actual bytes, you get enterprise-grade data management out of the box, with:.

Cloud Storage durability and simplified lifecycle management: Object context shares the same durability and consistency properties as the underlying Cloud Storage object. It travels automatically with the object during copy, move, and replication operations and is automatically removed when the object is deleted — no more cleanup jobs!

Fine-grained IAM governance: Using IAM, administrators can control who can read, add, revision, or remove object context.

Fast object filtering and serving: Applications can filter object listings directly by object context key-value pairs or read context metadata alongside objects, in order to serve richer experiences.

Turnkey multimodal analytics in BigQuery: You can easily configure your object context to natively flow into BigQuery via Storage Insights datasets, allowing data teams to run SQL analytics, build dashboards, and join unstructured file insights with structured enterprise tables, without writing a single line of ETL code.

Early customers are already putting object enrichments to work across key business scenarios:.

Creative asset search and media archives: Marketing, retail, and media organizations manage petabytes of creative image assets, where finding a specific asset, e.g., "a red car driving at sunset" or "a vintage convertible in the desert during golden hour", requires rich semantic metadata. Object enrichments automatically generates descriptive labels in object context, which can then be indexed into a vector database or BigQuery to power accurate retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications and asset-discovery agents.

Automated trust, safety, and content moderation: Social platforms, marketplaces, and digital media pipelines scan millions of user uploads and supplier catalogs every day for explicit content. Historically, scaling this for every single upload has been cost-prohibitive, but not anymore. With object enrichments, you can process 10 million images for just $700.

Training data curation for frontier AI: Autonomous driving, smart home, and robotics companies capture hundreds of millions of raw camera and sensor files. They often need targeted data samples for specific fine-tuning scenarios, which make up only a tiny fraction of their corpus. By enriching raw captures in place with object detection and image labeling models and then querying the resulting metadata in BigQuery, ML engineers can pinpoint exact training cohorts in minutes rather than months.

Multimodal analytics: Combine insights from images and documents with structured business data to drive personalization, fraud detection, and trend discovery — for example, analyzing customer uploaded images of the product alongside their comments and recent sales data.

Industry observers note that object enrichments is available in preview today in the Cloud Storage console and through the Cloud Storage API. To get started, check out the following resources.

Read the documentation: Learn how to configure an enrichments job and use object contexts.

Analyze in BigQuery: Set up Storage Insights datasets and query your enrichments alongside your BigQuery business data.

Connect your agents: Pair object enrichments and object context with the Cloud Storage MCP server to give agents secure, IAM-scoped access to your data and its context.

Review pricing: See Cloud Storage pricing for details.

Gemini enrichments: Reach out to us at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality.

Start building: Head to the Cloud Storage console to enrich your first bucket in just three clicks.

  • Here are a few examples of workloads that benefit from higher pod density:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports higher pod density per node on EKS-orchestrated clusters, allowing you to get more out of every instance. This leaves more room for your applications alongside system DaemonSets for monitoring, logging, and security, and helps increase GPU, CPU and memory utilization on nodes, allowing you to run the same work using fewer instances.

As you schedule more pods, the Amazon VPC CNI automatically adds network capacity to the node. Autoscaling with Karpenter also supports the higher pod capacity, so new nodes take on more pods as your cluster scales out.

Here are a few examples of workloads that benefit from higher pod density:.

Model inference - Serve more model replicas or more models from each GPU instance, including on smaller types such as ml.g5 and ml.g6.

Interactive development - Host more notebooks, IDEs, and data science environments on each node.

GPU partitioning - Use all the Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) slices on instances such as ml.p5en.48xlarge, where each slice runs its own pod.

Operators and Controllers - Run operators, controllers, and observability agents on CPU nodes alongside your workloads, without crowding them out.

Sources indicate that this feature is available for HyperPod EKS-orchestrated clusters in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available. To get started, update your cluster's IAM permissions, cluster software, and Amazon VPC CNI add-on. To learn more, please check the documentation.

Hyderabad, Jakarta, Melbourne, Mumbai, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, Central, Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Stockholm, N. Virginia, Ohio, Oregon, N. California, Canada (Central), São Paulo.

arXiv:2611.24845v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Existing AI agents can retrieve information, call tools, run experiments, and produce multi-step outputs. Yet most are built around relatively static workflows and struggle to preserve reliable state as the environment changes. Financial trading makes this limitation especially consequential: prices, news, market conditions, portfolio positions, and available capital evolve continuously. A result is useful only when it remains tied to the correct time, data snapshot, and execution context. We present Vibe-Trading, a comprehensive agent-native trading framework and all-in-one workspace for building, evaluating, and evolving agents for financial trading. It unifies market research, financial data, strategy generation, backtesting, portfolio analysis, paper trading, multi-agent collaboration, and optional broker execution. Its central contribution is an architecture that keeps results, evidence, research history, and trading authority connected throughout the research-to-action process. Each result retains its source, temporal scope, configuration, and producing run. Shared evidence grounding enables verification, versioned research records support reproducible continuation, and an explicit authority gate separates strategy research from live execution. Together, these designs provide a practical foundation for trading agents whose results can be traced, reproduced, and acted on only under explicit authority.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (202 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: F$^3$: What Makes Good Experience in World-Action Models?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (202 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.24708v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Deployed world-action models (WAMs) can keep improving only if they make good use of their own experience. Existing methods supply retrieved rollouts or demonstrations to the policy as context, yet such experience often turns previously solved tasks into failures. What, then, makes good experience for a WAM? We show that experience is valuable only in use: its value depends not on whether the source rollout succeeded but on what is stored, when it is used, and where it enters the policy. We therefore propose F$^3$, which makes these three decisions with Form, Fit, and Fusion. Form compresses successful and failed rollouts alike into short, verified operation records; Fit teaches the policy to read a record and to predict when it helps; Fusion injects the record's images, text and actions into the policy as a prefix and an action prior. Trained once on only 200 examples and deployed with a growing experience library, the model achieves state-of-the-art results on MolmoSpaces and RoboLab without any training on RoboLab: over native Cosmos 3 Nano, it raises success by 12.0 pp and 10.8 pp, reduces steps to success by 12.2% and 11.3%, and cuts regressions by 57%.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (176 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Depth Before Breadth: Reverse-to-Forward Curriculum with Advantage Decomposition for LLM Agent

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (176 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.24697v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, learning from sparse terminal rewards makes credit assignment and exploration difficult. We approach these challenges through a policy-induced capability region, the set of states from which the current policy can reliably complete a task. Near its boundary, an agent may need only a few actions to reach a more solvable state, even when the goal remains distant. This reduces long-horizon learning to two coupled subproblems of reaching that state and completing the task from there. We address them with paired advantages and a progressive reverse-to-forward curriculum. The advantages provide separate signals for reaching more solvable states and completing the task from them, while the curriculum expands the capability region backward along successful reference trajectories and then into off-reference states through on-policy exploration. On ALFWorld and WebShop, our method outperforms competitive agentic RL methods at both model scales, achieving success rates of 90.1%/96.1% and 80.2%/82.6% with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, respectively.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that you can now replicate data in Amazon S3 buckets with fewer replication rules using two new S3 Replication capabilities, exclusions and Multi-Region key resolution.
  • Sources indicate that with exclusions, you can replicate an entire bucket while skipping specific prefixes or tagged objects, such as logs or experimental data.
  • Sources indicate that exclusions and Multi-Region key resolution are optional and available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions.

Industry observers note that you can now replicate data in Amazon S3 buckets with fewer replication rules using two new S3 Replication capabilities, exclusions and Multi-Region key resolution. Buckets that many tenants or applications share often need many rules to skip certain data or to match encryption keys in each AWS Region. With these capabilities, customers who manage multi-tenant and shared buckets can replace many replication rules with a single rule.

Sources indicate that with exclusions, you can replicate an entire bucket while skipping specific prefixes or tagged objects, such as logs or experimental data. With Multi-Region key resolution, S3 Replication encrypts each replica with the matching AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) Multi-Region key in the destination Region, so replicas meet the same encryption requirements as their source objects. For example, a bucket that stores data for hundreds of tenants, each with its own Multi-Region key, can replicate with a single rule, including tenants you add later.

Sources indicate that exclusions and Multi-Region key resolution are optional and available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions. To get started, use the AWS SDKs, AWS CLI, S3 API, or S3 console. To learn more, visit the S3 Replication product page and Replicating objects within and across Regions in the S3 User Guide.

Evaluating 14 models on the same films with their selected primary harnesses reveals complementary strengths in game quality, adaptation, and player experience. These findings identify two linked priorities for film-to-game adaptation: preserving source situations that can support gameplay and connecting retained content to player actions and consequences.

#12280. Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1836 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1836 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage.
  • It has been revealed that our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap.
  • Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this proposal includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

It has been revealed that our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this proposal includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern shows up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

In a recent development, A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

Sources indicate that this is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

Industry observers note that provenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

It has been revealed that the verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a new setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

According to recent reports, we tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts noted 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

Recent findings suggest that we ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Recent findings suggest that binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an crucial area for improvement.

In a recent development, we also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This reveals it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

Industry observers note that that adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Industry observers note that practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval states "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Recent findings suggest that hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the problem well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;.

Industry observers note that like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

It has been revealed that however, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

  • Starting in 2027, staff at the more than 650 businesses that presently use DYNO will be able to manage both an occupational pension (bAV) and an AVD in a single place.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DYNO, an Offenburg-based digital occupational pension provider, has joined forces with lemon.markets, a Berlin-based Brokerage-as-a-Service FinTech, to add Germany’s new state-subsidised retirement investment account, the Altersvorsorgedepot (AVD), to its platform.

Starting in 2027, staff at the more than 650 businesses that presently use DYNO will be able to manage both an occupational pension (bAV) and an AVD in a single place. lemon.markets will run the brokerage and custody backbone for the AVD, handling everything from opening accounts and safekeeping assets to processing subsidies and tax.

Industry observers note that the move turns DYNO from a provider focused only on occupational pensions into a broader retirement platform. Until now it has offered ETF-based bAV contracts without commission, and the AVD extends its reach into private retirement saving. Its “Pension Intelligence” tool combines the statutory, occupational and private pension pillars in a single view, helping employees understand how to maximise employer contributions and government subsidies.

Recent findings suggest that through its integrated API platform, lemon.markets manages the full investment chain behind the AVD. As an investment firm licensed by BaFin, it supplies a compliant, off-the-shelf private retirement account, meaning DYNO does not need to build its own execution, custody, subsidy or tax functions.

Sources indicate that DYNO retains ownership of its relationships with employers and staff and operates the customer-facing interface. For lemon.markets, the deal represents its first step into occupational pensions and opens up employers as a fresh distribution route.

It has been revealed that DYNO was set up in 2021 by Marc Karkossa and Luis Weber and applies the neobroker approach to workplace pensions. It describes itself as the first digital platform allowing firms and their staff to arrange commission-free, ETF-based pension contracts directly, which it says cuts costs, improves transparency and delivers stronger long-term returns.

lemon.markets gives banks, asset managers and FinTechs access to capital markets via a single API, works with firms such as Pleo, Holvi, Optio and Tomorrow, and has been part of the dwpbank Group since August 2025, which holds more than €2.4 trillion in assets under custody.

Sources indicate that DYNO co-founder and CEO Marc Karkossa said, “Retirement saving tends to work best for people who already know their way around finance. Many employees would benefit from a good retirement product but never get one, simply because nobody guides them.

It has been revealed that “We built DYNO to change that. With the AVD, we now cover a second product and show each employee how to use both to get the most out of employer contributions and state subsidies.”.

lemon.markets founder and CEO Max Linden remarked, “Whether someone gets a good occupational pension should not depend on union membership, a collective agreement or a works council. Most employees in small and mid-sized companies meet none of these conditions. Bringing bAV and AVD together on one platform makes retirement savings easier to manage. That is what DYNO is building for 2027, with lemon.markets as its infrastructure partner.”.

Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (185 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.24650v2 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Small language models (SLMs) can run on commodity hardware and support privacy-preserving, on-premises clinical deployment, but their medical explanations are often short and poorly structured compared with large language models. Recent supervised approaches such as Meerkat transfer chain-of-thought reasoning into 7B-8B backbones, yet their training objective does not directly target the style or organization of the generated rationales. Building on the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B backbone, we investigate whether a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) step can improve explanation structure without human preference labels. We apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with LoRA adaptation to 2000 Meerkat-derived medical prompts, guided by a simple self-supervised reward that favors longer, lexically diverse, and well-punctuated responses while penalizing very short ones. Training for about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU yields a stable increase in the average reward. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show that the RL-tuned model produces longer, more organized, multi-point explanations while preserving the underlying medical content. We discuss the promise and the limitations of self-rewarded RL for shaping the style of medical explanations.
