It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.23817v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Coding agents now write whole codebases in long autonomous runs, guided mainly by whether their tests pass. Yet passing tests alone does not reveal accumulating complexity or gaps in test coverage, which then persist as agents extend their own code. We introduce metrics-in-the-loop, an inference-time intervention that gives agents in-flight feedback: cheap, automatically computed code metrics injected into the agent's context during the trajectory. After each code-changing agent turn, we insert short feedback messages naming changed functions whose cyclomatic complexity exceeds a limit (complexity feedback) or changed lines that are skipped by tests (coverage feedback), giving the agent the opportunity to refactor code or strengthen tests before continuing. We run extensive experiments and ablations comparing several interventions across three long-horizon coding benchmarks and four strong models. We find that complexity feedback significantly reduces erosion, a measure of complexity concentration of code, without affecting held-out correctness of the code. Broadly, our experiments investigate a practical form of agent "re-railing", where timely, actionable measurements redirect agents before weaknesses become the foundation they keep building on. As agents scale to codebases with millions of lines, such interventions become critical to sustaining effective development and long-term code maintainability.

arXiv:2611.23810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal agents largely rely on generic tools such as cropping, search, and code execution, leaving specialist vision models outside their tool space. However, bringing such a model into an already trained agent is not straightforward. The challenge is to learn each new tool efficiently while retaining the ability to use existing ones. This work proposes COTEX, continual tool-space extension learning, that adds new tools at efficient adapter-level cost. COTEX locates two sets of parameter directions; one triggers a tool call and thereby opens a multi-turn reasoning trajectory, while the other determines which tool is chosen. The adapter of a new tool is restricted to the calling directions that leave earlier tool choices unaffected by orthogonal constraint. We further introduce a protocol that converts specialist models' existing task-specific annotations into verified tool-use trajectories. Experiments on two representative agents and three specialist tools show gains on ten vision-language benchmarks, with at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS Glue ETL now offers the Apache Spark Optimization Agent, which analyzes completed Spark job runs and delivers cost and performance optimization recommendations within minutes.
  • The agent takes the job's configuration, logs, and Spark telemetry together with your chosen goal and returns recommendations computed by a deterministic recommendation engine.
  • Sources indicate that the Apache Spark Optimization Agent is available at no additional charge for AWS Glue versions 4.0 and later in all Regions where AWS Glue is available, except the AWS GovCloud (US) and China Regions.

AWS Glue ETL now offers the Apache Spark Optimization Agent, which analyzes completed Spark job runs and delivers cost and performance optimization recommendations within minutes. You can select a cost or performance goal, and the agent returns specific configuration changes with the telemetry evidence and reasoning behind each suggestion. You can use the agent on any completed job run from the AWS Glue console, or from your own tools through the Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio MCP Server.

The agent takes the job's configuration, logs, and Spark telemetry together with your chosen goal and returns recommendations computed by a deterministic recommendation engine. The engine reads all job artifacts together to identify what is driving runtime and cost: too little parallelism, a skewed join key, memory pressure forcing spill, idle executors, or capacity provisioned beyond what the job uses. When cost and performance trade off, the agent improves the metric you chose while keeping any regression of the other within defined limits. The engine also checks best practices such as platform-level improvements like upgrading to a newer AWS Glue version or using AWS Graviton processors. Each recommendation is labeled by the area it modifies: infrastructure, Spark configuration, code, or data layout. All access is authenticated with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and logged in AWS CloudTrail.

Sources indicate that the Apache Spark Optimization Agent is available at no additional charge for AWS Glue versions 4.0 and later in all Regions where AWS Glue is available, except the AWS GovCloud (US) and China Regions. To get started, see Apache Spark Optimization Agent for Amazon EMR and AWS Glue and the blog post - Introducing the Apache Spark optimization agent for Amazon EMR Serverless and AWS Glue ETL.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.23751v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a shared, domain-general source of decision points. Offline, AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions across over 1,000 public skills, gathers execution-grounded trajectory states inside isolated containers to construct Any-DP, and trains a single calibrated 4B pointer System-1 with label smoothing. At run time, compiled workflows resolve routine decisions in one forward pass and fall back to System-2 when confidence falls below a calibrated threshold. Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, and maintains performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

It has been revealed that LFM2 demonstrated that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

Industry observers note that the payoff reveals at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Industry observers note that every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:.

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Recent findings suggest that reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

According to recent reports, reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

It has been revealed that LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

In a recent development, we adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that amazon OpenSearch Memory is available today in US East (N.

It has been revealed that today, AWS revealed the general availability of Amazon OpenSearch Memory, a new serverless capability in Amazon OpenSearch Service for adding persistent memory to AI agents. OpenSearch Memory stores agent interactions as searchable events, derives useful memories, and retrieves relevant context across sessions, so agents can recall prior decisions, earlier interactions, and user preferences without replaying the full conversation history to the model. Customers can give agents long-term memory without provisioning infrastructure or building separate extraction, indexing, consolidation, and retrieval systems.

OpenSearch Memory stores the original events verbatim, makes them searchable within seconds, and asynchronously derives structured memories. It manages the full memory lifecycle, including extraction, embedding, indexing, consolidation (adding, updating, or skipping memories as fresh information arrives), and retrieval using keyword, semantic, and hybrid search. Customers control access with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) for each memory store, with actor and session scoping, and can set expiration periods for events and memories. Because it is serverless, there are no clusters to provision, instance types to choose, or indexes to create, and capacity for extraction and search scales automatically.

It has been revealed that amazon OpenSearch Memory is available today in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo) Regions. For pricing details about Amazon OpenSearch Memory, visit the pricing page.

According to recent reports, to learn more about Amazon OpenSearch Memory, see the technical documentation and launch blog. You can get started by visiting the technical launch blog that details how to add persistent memory to your agents with Amazon OpenSearch Memory.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that stage-level progress gives you a clear, detailed view of where each deployment stands.
  • To get started, open the Progress view for a stack set operation in the CloudFormation console, or use the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs.

AWS CloudFormation StackSets now indicates stage-by-stage progress for deployments across accounts and AWS Regions, whether you target tens of accounts or thousands. You can follow each deployment as it progresses and take action when needed, without waiting for it to finish. StackSets lets you consistently apply the same infrastructure or application components, such as networking and security settings, across many accounts and Regions in one operation. With this launch, you can see how many stack instances are deployed, how many remain, and which ones need attention. This gives you confidence that a rollout is on track at every stage.

Recent findings suggest that stage-level progress gives you a clear, detailed view of where each deployment stands. Previously, a StackSets deployment indicated an overall status while it ran. Now, StackSets also reports progress for two stages. The first is role provisioning, which prepares access in each target account of a service-managed stack set. The second is stack deployment, which deploys your template as a stack instance in each account and Region. For example, in a deployment to 2,000 accounts in 3 Regions, you can see that role provisioning is complete and stack deployment has reached 40 percent, with 2,400 stack instances completed and 3,600 pending. Progress for each Region and the result of each stage remain available after the deployment completes.

Latest Update: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (290 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.23700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinicians reviewing a diagnostic work-up will ask what was considered at each step and why the assessment changed. Agents powered by free text can reach physician-level diagnostic accuracy, but their written reasoning does not always reflect the factors that went into the decision. Here, we present Decision2Care, a decision agent that works up the acutely ill patient without producing any text. A decision model assigns a probability to each permitted EHR action, and fixed rules carry out the most probable one. We evaluated Decision2Care on the records of 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases. Decision2Care reached a diagnostic accuracy of 86.5%, compared with 86.1% for the MIRA-v2 agent, and required a median of 2.2 s per work-up, compared with 92-100 s. Each work-up tracked which options Decision2Care was considering at each step. In 10 of the 12 diseases, the differential diagnosis changed most at the test on which the guideline bases the diagnosis. Where Decision2Care was most confident after a single work-up, all but four of its diagnoses were correct (98.5%). We traced each of these four errors back to a single imaging report. Three of them were corrected when that report was removed. The same kind of decision was used to select the treatments, and Decision2Care's drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than MIRA-v2's. In emergency patients, its prediction of death was comparable to that of three intensivists on the same cases. In five of the eight intensive care cohorts, it exceeded the best of the three 24-h severity scores within 2-6 h of records. Our results show that decision agents can carry out clinical work-ups while recording the options, probabilities, and execution rules behind each action for audit.

Breaking: Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • They write, summarize, translate, and call tools.
  • In a recent development, say a customer calls your support line.
  • In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

In a recent development, say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

It has been revealed that computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

In a recent development, the package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

In a recent development, the steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Sources indicate that parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Recent findings suggest that qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

In a recent development, to add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

In a recent development, when you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

Recent findings suggest that the diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

Recent findings suggest that the diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

In a recent development, what's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

According to recent reports, apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

It has been revealed that the app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

In a recent development, the session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

Sources indicate that you use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

It has been revealed that language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

It has been revealed that like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

It has been revealed that both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

In a recent development, try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Challenges and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (257 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.23678v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score indicates nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. Across six ML tasks, from synthetic logistic regression to language-model training, and 1,445 trials, the same contract applied unchanged. The ledger exposed failures that a task score hides: a no-memory arm in which all 120 trials failed, a benchmark adapter whose bounded proposals ran out, and a reset failure that reproducibility hashes revealed, after which the affected campaigns were rerun. In a matched counterfactual, a loop that logs only successful trials left no record of 43 of 50 trials, while the governed ledger recorded all 50. Memory ablations show that memory's effect on repeated bad proposals depends on the task. We release the ledgers of all 1,445 trials, so that every number reported for them can be recomputed.

AWS AppConfig rolls out support for managing native AI model and AI prompt configuration

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, today, AWS AppConfig introduces two new configuration profile types to help you manage the settings for your generative AI applications: AI model invocation configurations, and AI prompt configurations.
  • AI model invocation configurations store the settings your application uses to call an AI model.
  • Sources indicate that you can roll out a change to these gradually, for example to 10%, then 20%, then 30% of your traffic.

According to recent reports, today, AWS AppConfig introduces two new configuration profile types to help you manage the settings for your generative AI applications: AI model invocation configurations, and AI prompt configurations. You can now change model settings and prompts while your application is running, without redeploying code. These updates use AWS AppConfig's safe deployment practices, including gradual rollouts and automatic rollback. This can allow you to move faster and safer, and avoid unexpected behaviors and tokenomics results with rapidly evolving AI solutions.

AI model invocation configurations store the settings your application uses to call an AI model. These include the model identifier, inference parameters such as temperature and maximum tokens, and messages such as system prompts and example conversation turns. Provider-specific options are managed in custom parameters, so the same schema works across AI providers. Similarly, AI prompt configurations store prompts as separately versioned artifacts. You can update  and optimize a prompt on its own,without changing the model configuration, and reuse it across multiple applications. This allows for powerful prompt engineering.

Sources indicate that you can roll out a change to these gradually, for example to 10%, then 20%, then 30% of your traffic. Along the way, you can measure the change's effect on operational metrics, customer experience, and token usage. If an alarm in Amazon CloudWatch, Datadog, Latest Relic, or another observability solution goes off during the rollout, AWS AppConfig can automatically roll the change back to the previous state.

In a recent development, AI model invocation and AI prompt configurations are available today in all AWS Regions where AWS AppConfig is available, at no additional cost. To get started, see Creating an AI model invocation configuration profile and Creating an AI prompt configuration profile in the AWS AppConfig User Guide.

arXiv:2611.23639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In cosmology, surveys span different sky regions and wavelength ranges, resulting in uneven modality coverage across observational datasets. Such heterogeneity can be addressed through either multimodal foundation models (FMs), which learn shared embedding spaces, or independently learned modality embeddings combined via late fusion. We investigate whether the latter provides an adaptive alternative to FM-based scientific retrieval. We evaluate this approach on a galaxy retrieval task spanning diverse modalities--history of star formation, spectra of light emitted, and multi-wavelength observations from two telescopes--comparing an FM baseline with separately trained embeddings fused through multi-objective optimization based on Pareto optimality. We find that the FM baseline achieves strong embedding-space proximity, but our method preserves modality-specific distance structure that allows scientists to inspect which physical signals drive similarity. Our method also achieves improved fidelity in raw-data space: across six measured properties, its nearest neighbor is 8% closer to the query on average than that retrieved by kNN in the FM embedding space (spread 0.128 vs. 0.139). These results suggest that multi-objective retrieval can surface astrophysically coherent candidates that single-objective search alone may overlook.

Latest Update: Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1607 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • Sources indicate that there are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

Sources indicate that there are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super key for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

In a recent development, mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That mentioned, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

According to recent reports, on coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

According to recent reports, cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

In a recent development, the Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

In a recent development, amazon S3 Tables replication now lets you make a read-only replica of your Apache Iceberg table a standalone, writable table with a single API call. S3 Tables replication keeps read-only replica tables in sync with your source tables across table buckets, AWS Regions, and accounts. Instead of copying a replica into a newly introduced table, you can promote it in place to move writes to another Region.

Sources indicate that when you disassociate a replica from replication, the standalone table keeps its namespace and table name, so your queries and pipeline code carry over when you point your applications at it. The promoted table then works like an S3 table you created, and you can use it as a source for fresh replicas.

According to recent reports, this capability is available in all AWS Regions where S3 Tables replication is supported. You can use the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or S3 Tables API. For pricing details, visit the Amazon S3 pricing page. To learn more, see the S3 Tables overview page and documentation.

arXiv:2611.23611v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Tool runtimes can lower an agent-selected operation into a hidden parallel graph, reducing latency and context while risking semantic mistranslation. We introduce RefinementGuard: translation validation for hidden, effectful agent-tool lowerings, coupled to artifact-bound, fail-closed runtime admission. Qualification compares a candidate graph with an independent reference on isolated state using explicit parent-operation obligations. We evaluate two repository-level contracts, bug localization and patch validation, on controlled repositories. Among 100 activated, non-equivalent development/qualification faults adjudicated by one human, parent-semantic validation rejects 49/100 (operator-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [33.7%, 64.8%]). The objective is selective admission, not maximum mutation rejection: exact equality rejects 100/100 faults but also all 60 valid variants, whereas obligation-based validation accepts 60/60; its 51 residual misses identify concrete specification gaps. On a frozen disjoint input split, the held-out B2-B3 result is localization-only because 21 patch mutants fail structurally; B3 rejects 38/56 localization defects. In a controlled asynchronous-delay regime, the localization serial/guarded median-latency ratio is 4.50x, and hidden execution exposes 74.3% less parent-visible context than visible execution. Patch validation demonstrates no demonstrated speedup; zero-delay runs expose overhead. End-to-end qualification thus detects lower-layer misses while preserving localization's parallelism.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.23588v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Enterprise LLM agents operate in dynamic environments where foundation models evolve rapidly, workflows update frequently, and deployments need to satisfy accuracy and cost requirements. We propose ARISE (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation), a practical memory architecture in which the agent's memory evolves from its own failures without updating model weights, tools, or workflow logic. ARISE uses the model itself or a teacher model to attribute the failures and propose corrections. Then, ARISE keeps the corrections as retrievable micro memory, consolidates them into macro rules, and accepts a rule update only if held-out accuracy rises. Across 14 enterprise-workflow domains from SOP-Bench and $\tau^2$-bench using 5 models, ARISE-Teacher, which uses Claude Opus 4.6 for attribution and consolidation, gains 10.9 pp over the baseline on SOP-Bench and 5.8 pp on $\tau^2$-bench. 📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (193 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.23572v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Food insecurity creates a pressing need for guidance that helps households find usable food resources and assess food choices in light of their circumstances. Such guidance must connect eligibility requirements, practical access constraints, and dietary needs rather than return isolated listings or generic nutritional advice. Multi-agent food assistants can coordinate these tasks, with uncertainty indicating when clarification or verification is needed before a recommendation. However, uncertainty can be lost across agent handoffs, allowing tentative interpretations to propagate as facts and obscuring opportunities for correction. Moreover, confidence that a service requirement has been interpreted correctly is not confidence that a recommendation satisfies the user's needs; local confidence cannot simply be reused as downstream reliability. We introduce an inference-time, receiver-conditioned clarification framework that preserves shared premise identities and replays consistent interpretations across dependent agents. Each receiver exposes admissible decisions and remaining evidence obligations, so question relevance reflects both decision changes and missing support. Information questions and user-confirmable fallback adjustments are evaluated together with their anticipated follow-up interactions under shared budgets. This structure connects clarification to jointly supported looks for resource navigation, nutritional reasoning, and supply-side planning.

Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1308 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
  • According to recent reports, today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

According to recent reports, today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Recent findings suggest that participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

It has been revealed that the U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to initiative for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

Recent findings suggest that but making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

It has been revealed that the demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Industry observers note that figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an key part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved vital in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support upcoming research that others can build upon.

Sources indicate that this is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

According to recent reports, to explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Sources indicate that participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Sources indicate that beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

In a recent development, the CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be unveiled through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

Industry observers note that we also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

arXiv:2611.23564v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: When LLM agents pass intermediate judgments downstream without uncertainty, later decisions may treat tentative assumptions as facts. Effective uncertainty propagation must preserve information for correction and revision inherited beliefs as new evidence arrives. Yet scalar scores omit information needed for revision, while detailed descriptions and reflection incur additional costs. We introduce Latent Uncertainty, a latent-space estimator that preserves uncertainty-relevant information without lengthy descriptions. Building on this, we propose LProp (Latent Uncertainty Propagation), which revises inherited answer distributions using latent representations and new evidence without additional trajectory sampling. We evaluate both methods across multiple-choice, yes/no, open-ended question answering, and mathematical reasoning tasks. Our approach outperforms baselines on most metrics, while LProp achieves the lowest mean inference-token usage in all eight propagation settings. Matched feature ablations further demonstrate that inherited latent content improves error recovery beyond answer probabilities or model capacity alone.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (239 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2611.23560v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Personality is only weakly and inconsistently signaled by written language, and existing text-based methods typically combine language-model and psycholinguistic representations at the input or decision level. It remains open whether a more deliberate combination of the two views, and a decomposition of the prediction target, can recover more of the signal. We present a three-phase framework for estimating Substantial Five personality domain scores from life-narrative interview text. It encodes text and psycholinguistic features separately and combines them by concatenation or by a learned weighting, decomposes each domain into contrastively trained facet embeddings instead of predicting the domain directly, and pools the facet embeddings by attention into a domain-level prediction. We compare end-to-end with staged training and ablate the input modalities, their combination, and the facet-pooling strategy. On 1,332 participants from the St. Louis Personality and Aging Network (SPAN) study, facet embeddings reach AUC up to 0.740, and domain-level R2 reaches 0.328, highest for Openness. End-to-end training gives lower error than staged training in every domain, and attention pooling gives the lowest error in every domain. Combining the two views lowers error relative to text alone for Conscientiousness and Agreeableness, whereas a learned weighting of the views demonstrates no consistent advantage over concatenation. The framework provides facet- level predictions that a domain-only model cannot, and it improves modestly on a regression from the raw features in four of the five domains.

Industry observers note that you can now associate AWS Network Firewall with NAT Gateway and use it both as an explicit proxy and a transparent firewall with native network address translation. You can use this capability with existing Network Firewall features to filter traffic to and from your applications and prevent data exfiltration and malware injection.

Sources indicate that AWS Network Firewall is a stateful, managed, network firewall and intrusion detection and prevention service for your VPC. Customers use it to filter their traffic and secure AWS resources. With this launch, you can configure Network Firewall with native NAT Gateway association and use it for both explicit proxy and routed filtering functionalities. Both these functionalities are governed by a single security policy that you maintain centrally. This capability works with existing Network Firewall features including managed rule groups from Amazon or Marketplace, active threat defense, Geo-IP filtering, URL and domain category filtering, container attribute-based rules for Amazon EKS and Amazon ECS, etc. You can access Network Firewall from any VPC in your environment, even the ones with overlapping IP CIDR space, using VPC endpoints. Your traffic reaches the firewall via the VPC endpoint and the filtered traffic exits directly from the NAT Gateway using its IP address.

Recent findings suggest that this capability is available in US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Frankfurt), Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Thailand), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Europe (Spain). 📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (251 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.23520v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-series sensing increasingly relies on neural networks, yet deployment on resource-constrained microcontrollers remains challenging. Aggressive model compression can reduce accuracy, while restricting weights to multiplication-free representations introduces further losses. We present BeFit, an end-to-end framework that shifts model capacity from weights to learnable Bernstein polynomial activations. BeFit (i) finds compact Bernstein-activated convolutional neural networks (BeCNNs) through hardware-aware neural architecture search and trains them via knowledge distillation; (ii) projects their weights to multiplication-free codes, freezes the codes, and recovers the resulting accuracy loss through the learnable activations; and (iii) generates model-specific kernels that exploit the projected weights for multiplication-free convolutions. On human activity recognition, BeCNNs are 2.75 percentage points (pp) more accurate on average than ReLU CNNs of identical architecture. On a TI CC3220SF (Cortex-M4), weight projection speeds BeCNNs up by 2.2x on average while losing 0.8 pp, compared with 2.4 pp for ReLU CNNs. Against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN reference model running on TensorFlow Lite Micro with CMSIS-NN, the unprojected BeCNN achieves 1.0 pp higher accuracy, 2.2x lower latency, and 6.4x lower flash, while the projected model remains within 1.0 pp of the reference accuracy and runs 5.9x faster. In emulation on a RISC-V core without a hardware multiplier, the instruction-count reduction relative to the DS-CNN increases from 5.2x on the Cortex-M4 to 147x. BeFit also extends to transformers and MLPs, and across all tasks the final models stay within 1.56 pp of their float32 teachers on average.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

It has been revealed that granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

In a recent development, while we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this enhancement. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

Recent findings suggest that this pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

Breaking: GRAFT: Execution-Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (174 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.23509v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Automated agent design searches for executable architectures that improve LLM-based agent performance, with evolutionary methods using language-model crossover to recombine promising mechanisms for task decomposition, model coordination, and verification. This search, however, is typically guided by aggregate fitness alone, which hides the instance-level successes and failures behind each score. We introduce Execution Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design (GRAFT), which uses aggregate fitness for selection and survival and parent-specific execution evidence to guide semantic crossover with integrated mutation. Its feedback harness reuses bounded samples of successful and failed runs from fitness evaluation, withholding reference answers and requiring no additional task executions. We evaluate GRAFT across six reasoning and programming settings using open-weight optimizer and executor models. It achieves a mean test accuracy of 82.0%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.8% points. Controlled ablations show that adding execution evidence improves test accuracy with initialization, search rules, repair policies, and evaluation budgets held fixed. Our results support the value of parent-specific execution evidence for evolutionary agent design.

Industry observers note that amazon Inspector Code Security now supports GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) integration and private network connectivity for GHES and GitLab Self-Managed. Code Security is also launching automatic fix pull requests in public preview. Organizations that host GHES or GitLab Self-Managed in private networks can now connect through Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) configurations or AWS CodeConnections, so they can scan repositories without opening their firewalls to the entire AWS IP address range.

Amazon Inspector Code Security scans first-party application source code, third-party dependencies, and Infrastructure as Code for vulnerabilities in repositories on GitHub, GHES, and GitLab Self-Managed. With automatic fix pull requests, Amazon Inspector turns its suggested fix into a pull request that developers review and choose whether to merge, instead of applying the fix by hand. It opens pull requests only for high-confidence fixes to static application security testing (SAST) findings at or above a severity you set.

It has been revealed that these features are available in all 10 AWS Regions where Amazon Inspector Code Security is available: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and Asia Pacific (Singapore). To learn more, see the Amazon Inspector User Guide and the Amazon Inspector product page.
